dedupe_keys.name: internet traffic and routing in an isp after the 2011 great east japan earthquake

description: This post-event and recovery case examines how the internet behaved inside one large Japanese internet service provider after the earthquake and tsunami of 11 March 2011. Researchers at Internet Initiative Japan (IIJ) used traffic volume measurements and routing data from inside the ISP, together with routing data from a neighbouring ISP, to follow circuit failures and repairs over the following weeks. They found that, apart from the areas hit directly by the quake and tsunami, the internet was impressively resilient: many users in the Tokyo area found that voice networks failed while the internet kept working. Residential traffic in Miyagi prefecture fell sharply and recovered gradually, but this had little effect on total residential traffic in Japan; failures and repairs of circuits were clearly visible inside the network, yet little disruption could be seen from outside, and traffic on IIJ's eight redundant, over-provisioned links to the United States was rerouted when some of them failed. The paper was presented at the ACM CoNEXT 2011 Special Workshop on the Internet and Disasters, alongside a companion study of inter-domain rerouting after the quake. Coverage: one national ISP and its neighbours, March to April 2011. Format and access: ACM paper with a free author copy; the ISP's internal data are not public. Caveats: a single operator's view; routing seen from outside may hide local access failures. Simulation uses: network flow and rerouting under earthquake and tsunami damage, value of redundant international links and recovery curves for access networks. Related records: the Japanese ministry's record of telecom damage and countermeasures covers the same event across operators.
